nameStory: Maryland meadowbeauty gets its name from its stunning pink to purple flowers that truly are beautiful enough to grace any meadow. The 'Maryland' part refers to where botanists first formally described this species, though it actually grows throughout much of the eastern United States. The name 'meadowbeauty' perfectly captures how these colorful blooms can transform an ordinary wetland into something spectacular.
description: Maryland meadowbeauty is a colonial perennial herb that spreads to form patches in wet areas. It grows up to 2.5 feet tall with sturdy stems and produces eye-catching flowers that can be pink, purple, or white. The plant has a somewhat bushy appearance when mature, with opposite leaves and showy blooms that make it hard to miss when in flower. After blooming, it develops distinctive red, urn-shaped seed capsules that persist into fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large showy flowers, 1-2 inches wide, with 4 delicate petals in pink, purple, or white. The bright yellow or orange anthers (pollen-bearing parts) create a striking contrast against the petals and feel powdery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves with elongated, oval blades that have small teeth along the edges. The leaves feel somewhat rough and have prominent veins running from base to tip.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive red, urn-shaped capsules that develop after flowers fade. These feel papery when dry and contain small brownish seeds that rattle when shaken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Colonial growth pattern, meaning it spreads underground to form patches rather than growing as isolated plants. Stems are square in cross-section and feel sturdy when gently squeezed.

habitat: Maryland meadowbeauty thrives in wet, sandy or peaty soils in coastal plain areas of New England. Look for it in wet meadows, bog edges, pond margins, and sometimes in roadside ditches with consistent moisture. It prefers full sun to partial shade and is most commonly found in areas with acidic soils.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green shoots appearing from underground rhizomes. Leaves develop their characteristic opposite pattern and toothed edges.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the spectacular pink, purple, or white flowers appear. This is the best time for identification when the large, showy blooms with bright yellow anthers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the distinctive red urn-shaped seed capsules develop and ripen. These persistent capsules make identification possible even after blooming ends.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only the underground rhizome system. The dried seed capsules may persist and can still be found among dead vegetation.

funFact: Maryland meadowbeauty belongs to a tropical plant family (Melastomataceae) that includes over 4,000 species worldwide, mostly in Central and South America - making our New England meadowbeauties some of the northernmost representatives of this primarily tropical group!
confusionNotes: Maryland meadowbeauty is most likely confused with its close relative Virginia meadowbeauty, which also grows in New England wetlands. Maryland meadowbeauty tends to have paler flowers and slightly narrower leaves, but the differences are subtle and the two species often hybridize where they meet.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Maryland' meadowbeauty, this plant isn't limited to Maryland and actually grows throughout much of the eastern United States. The observation count of only 6 in New England suggests this is a relatively uncommon find here, making any sighting special for nature enthusiasts.
compareHints: Maryland meadowbeauty differs from Virginia meadowbeauty primarily in its flower color, which tends to be paler (often white or very pale pink) compared to Virginia meadowbeauty's typically deeper pink to purple blooms. Maryland meadowbeauty also has slightly narrower, more elongated leaves and tends to prefer more acidic, sandy soils than its Virginia cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia meadowbeauty can be distinguished from its close relative Maryland meadowbeauty by its habitat preferences and leaf shape.
